title: Reverse an array in-place (two-pointer swap from ends).

s1_definition.profdef: Reversing an array in-place swaps elements from the two ends moving inward, using one pointer at the start and one at the end that step toward each other and exchange their elements until they meet. It mutates the original array, uses only constant extra space, and runs in linear time because it performs about half the array length in swaps. No new array is allocated, which is the point of the in-place requirement.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose the National Bank of India has Rajesh's transaction history listed oldest-first, but the mobile app must show newest-first. Rather than copying into a second list, two clerks start at opposite ends of the same list, swap the two entries they are holding, then each take one step toward the middle and swap again, continuing until they meet in the centre. The single list ends up reversed with no second list needed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Put one pointer at each end, swap, step both inward, and stop when they meet.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reversing an array in-place swaps elements from the two ends moving inward, using one pointer at the start and one at the end that step toward each other and exchange their elements until they meet. It mutates the original array, uses only constant extra space, and runs in linear time because it performs about half the array length in swaps. No new array is allocated, which is the point of the in-place requirement.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose the National Bank of India has Rajesh's transaction history listed oldest-first, but the mobile app must show newest-first. Rather than copying into a second list, two clerks start at opposite ends of the same list, swap the two entries they are holding, then each take one step toward the middle and swap again, continuing until they meet in the centre. The single list ends up reversed with no second list needed.

**One line to remember:** Put one pointer at each end, swap, step both inward, and stop when they meet.

sections.s2_technical:
The two-pointer technique uses a left index starting at zero and a right index starting at the last position, which is the length minus one. While left is less than right, you swap the elements at left and right, then increment left and decrement right. When left is no longer less than right, the pointers have met or crossed, and the array is fully reversed.

The loop runs about half the length of the array, performing one swap each time, so it does roughly length over two swaps, which is linear time overall. It uses only a single temporary for the swap, so the extra space is constant, which satisfies the in-place requirement.

A subtle point is the stopping condition. You loop while left is strictly less than right. If the array has an odd length, the exact middle element stays in place and does not need swapping with itself, and the strict less-than condition naturally handles that because left and right meet exactly at the middle and the loop stops. If you wrote less-than-or-equal instead, you would swap the middle element with itself, which is harmless but wasteful, and if you continued past the middle you would reverse it back, so the strict condition is important.

A senior point is mutation versus a fresh copy. In-place reversal changes the caller's array, which is efficient but has a side effect that can surprise callers who still hold a reference. In production I document that the method mutates its argument, and when I need the original preserved I offer a separate method that returns a reversed copy. Choosing mutation or copy is a deliberate API decision, not an accident.

Another senior point is the standard library. For objects you can wrap the array as a list and call the library reverse, and streams can reverse too, but those allocate or box. For primitive arrays and for a true constant-space in-place reversal, the explicit two-pointer loop is the right tool, and it is exactly what interviewers want to see because it demonstrates pointer control.

A small finance-domain example: `int left = 0, right = txns.length - 1; while (left < right) { String t = txns[left]; txns[left] = txns[right]; txns[right] = t; left++; right--; }` reverses a transaction-id array in place so newest appears first.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores Rajesh's transaction references in an array in chronological order, oldest first, because that is how they are appended as they occur. The mobile app's activity screen must display them newest first. Reversing the array in place gives the newest-first order without allocating a second array, which matters on memory-constrained mobile backends serving many users. Reversing in place with two pointers is exactly this operation.

This is exactly how in-place reversal works in Java — two pointers start at the ends and swap inward until they meet.

Problem 2 — Some callers still need the original chronological array for audit, so mutating the shared array would corrupt their view. The service must offer a non-mutating variant that returns a reversed copy, leaving the original intact, so the audit path and the display path do not interfere.

What the code will do: an `ActivityService` class with `reverseInPlace(String[] txns)` that mutates the array using two pointers, and `reversedCopy(String[] txns)` that returns a new reversed array without touching the original. The demo reverses Rajesh's transaction references for display and shows the audit copy is untouched.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the chronological array is `TXN-001, TXN-002, TXN-003, TXN-004, TXN-005`.

Step 1: `reversedCopy` first makes a copy of the array so the original is safe. Then it calls `reverseInPlace` on the copy. left starts at `0` and right starts at `4`.

Step 2: left `0` is less than right `4`, so we swap positions zero and four. The copy becomes `TXN-005, TXN-002, TXN-003, TXN-004, TXN-001`. Then left becomes `1` and right becomes `3`.

Step 3: left `1` is less than right `3`, so we swap positions one and three. The copy becomes `TXN-005, TXN-004, TXN-003, TXN-002, TXN-001`. Then left becomes `2` and right becomes `2`.

Step 4: left `2` is not less than right `2`, so the loop stops. The middle element `TXN-003` was never swapped because it sits exactly in the centre of an odd-length array, which the strict less-than condition handles.

Step 5: `reversedCopy` returns the reversed copy as the display order, newest first. The original chronological array is still in its original order, so the audit path sees an untouched list. This is the whole reason for the copy variant.

Step 6: The demo then calls `reverseInPlace` directly on the original, which mutates it to newest-first as well, demonstrating the deliberate difference between mutating and non-mutating variants.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T16:00:00Z INFO Display (newest first): [TXN-005, TXN-004, TXN-003, TXN-002, TXN-001]
2026-10-26T16:00:00Z INFO Audit (unchanged original): [TXN-001, TXN-002, TXN-003, TXN-004, TXN-005]
2026-10-26T16:00:00Z INFO After in-place reverse: [TXN-005, TXN-004, TXN-003, TXN-002, TXN-001]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [TXN-001, TXN-002, TXN-003, TXN-004, TXN-005]
    │
    ▼
  reversedCopy → copy, then two-pointer reverse the copy
    │ left=0,right=4 → swap → [005,002,003,004,001]
    │ left=1,right=3 → swap → [005,004,003,002,001]
    │ left=2,right=2 → stop (middle stays)
    ▼
  copy = [005,004,003,002,001]   original UNCHANGED
    │
    ├─ display path uses copy (newest first)
    ├─ audit path uses original (chronological)
    └─ reverseInPlace(original) → mutates original too
    ▼
  Output: display reversed, audit intact (copy variant)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing an array in place uses the two-pointer technique. I put one index at the start and one at the end, and while the left index is less than the right I swap the two elements, then step the left index forward and the right index backward. When they meet, the array is reversed. It does about half the length in swaps, so it is linear time, and it uses a single temporary, so the extra space is constant, which is exactly what in-place means.

The detail I always get right is the stopping condition: I loop while left is strictly less than right. For an odd-length array the middle element sits exactly where the pointers meet and never needs swapping with itself, and the strict condition handles that cleanly. Using less-than-or-equal would either swap the middle with itself wastefully or, if I over-ran, reverse elements back.

The API decision I highlight is mutation versus copy. In-place reversal changes the caller's array, which is efficient but a side effect that can surprise code still holding the reference, so I document the mutation and provide a separate method that returns a reversed copy when the original must be preserved.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to present Rajesh's transaction references newest first on the mobile activity screen, where the stored order is oldest first. I use the non-mutating copy variant for display so the audit path still sees the original chronological array, and I expose the in-place variant for the memory-constrained path where mutation is acceptable. Explaining the two-pointer loop, the odd-length stopping condition, and the mutation-versus-copy choice shows the interviewer I understand pointer control and the API consequences of mutating shared data.
